articles.title: Fiji Petrel Search Concludes with No Sightings
articles.summary: A team of scientists has concluded a 10-day search for one of the world's rarest birds, but unfortunately, the elusive Fiji petrel remained out of sight.
articles.content: A team of scientists has concluded a 10-day search for one of the world's rarest birds, but unfortunately, the elusive Fiji petrel remained out of sight. The expedition was conducted in partnership with National Geographic Pristine Seas and BirdLife International, with support from NatureFiji-MareqetiViti. The critically endangered bird is believed to have fewer than 50 individuals remaining on Earth, making it a top conservation priority. Community members on Gau Island, where the search took place, have pledged to protect the montane forests that are thought to be the bird's nesting grounds. Researchers managed to capture an audio recording of the Fiji petrel's call during their investigation, providing valuable insight into the bird's behavior and habitat. This unique sound is a significant contribution to the study of this enigmatic species. A paper detailing the expedition has been published in Bird Conservation International, offering a comprehensive review of historical sightings of the Fiji petrel and the findings of the 2025 at-sea survey and tagging attempt. The comprehensive review of historical sightings of the Fiji petrel includes every confirmed sighting from 1855 to the present day, providing a detailed picture of the species' presence over time. Despite being spotted on land on Gau until the 2000s, the last confirmed land sighting occurred in 2012, and since then there have been no further sightings. At sea, the last confirmed sighting was during a scientific search in 2023. This lack of nesting sites is a rare occurrence among seabird species. We're racing against time to save the Fiji petrel, said Lindsay Young, vice president of research for Pristine Seas, who led the expedition. The team employed tried-and-true techniques night and day, but unfortunately, the bird eluded them throughout their 10-day search. Meanwhile, local communities are taking steps to protect the bird's habitat. The scientists spent over 12 hours per day scouring the skies during their 10-day at-sea search, mostly in daylight hours. When the sun was out, they used a technique called chumming, releasing bait and fish oil on the sea surface to try and attract the birds. Spotlighting efforts at night aimed to draw in the petrels, using two handheld spotlights to create a strong beam visible from afar and an audio recording of calls meant to attract the bird on repeat. A mere 16 confirmed sightings of the Fiji petrel on land and 22 at sea have been documented by researchers. This scarcity of data has contributed significantly to the mystery surrounding this enigmatic species. The lack of understanding about the bird's habits is staggering, with its breeding patterns, population size, and foraging behavior remaining largely unknown. The team had hoped to shed some light on these secrets through a tagging effort, but after 10 days of intense searching, they came up empty-handed. A crucial component of their research involved consulting with residents of Gau Island, who possess traditional knowledge about the bird that has been passed down through generations. Through this collaboration, the team gained access to an invaluable resource: the only known audio recording of the Fiji petrel's call. The Fiji petrel holds a special place in Fijian culture and is featured on the country's 20-dollar banknote. Its significance extends beyond its cultural importance, with locals singing lullabies about the bird that have been passed down through generations on Gau Island, Fiji's fifth-largest island. Oral histories shared by village chiefs on Gau Island reveal a stark contrast to the bird's current scarcity. The island was once teeming with seabirds, including the Fiji petrel and similar species. Chiefs recalled stories from their great-grandmothers about collecting seabird eggs from the lower montane slopes behind the village. These egg collections were often made during pregnancy, when eating the eggs was considered desirable for a healthy outcome. The abundance of seabirds has significantly decreased over time, leaving only the Fiji petrel as a recorded presence on Gau Island. Habitat degradation and invasive predators pose significant threats to the Fiji petrel's survival. Feral cats, rats, and pigs have ravaged the island's ecosystem, putting immense pressure on the remaining bird population. The recent expedition's lack of confirmed sightings has highlighted the perilous status of the Fiji petrel. External factors such as a cyclone that passed south of the area during the survey period and a strong El Niño event may also be contributing to the bird's absence. Scientists acknowledge that one survey is not enough to paint an accurate picture, but they cannot deny the real risk that the Fiji petrel may be slipping away. The Fiji petrel's elusive nature has left scientists scrambling to confirm its existence after a 10-day search yielded no conclusive evidence of the bird's presence. Despite the challenges, conservation efforts are underway to protect the bird's habitat and prevent further decline in its population. Communities are working together to safeguard the areas where the Fiji petrel is known to nest and feed, with hopes that their efforts will help stabilize the species' numbers. The search for the Fiji petrel has been ongoing, but the bird's ability to evade detection has made it a difficult target for researchers. articles.title: US Flights Resume After Nationwide Ground Stop Due to Airspace Alert
articles.summary: A nationwide ground stop was issued due to an unusual alert in US airspace, stranding or en route hundreds of thousands of passengers over a four-hour period.
articles.content: US flights resumed their operations over the weekend after a nationwide stop due to an unusual alert issued in US airspace, leaving hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded or en route to destinations. The unprecedented incident marked just the second time such an alert had been issued since the 9/11 attacks, which targeted some of the world's busiest airspaces. The move came as a surprise to both airline staff and passengers, with many being pulled off planes mere moments before departure due to the unclear situation unfolding around them. Air traffic control facilities were at the center of the issue, with officials citing telecommunications problems tied to outdated equipment used for decades as the primary cause. There was no indication of any foul play or intentional disruption to air travel. As the ground stop lasted for four hours, passengers faced significant disruptions and cancellations. The incident led authorities to stress that returning to normal operations would take time. The Secretary of Transportation, Sean Duffy, emphasized that restoring full functionality at air traffic control facilities was a top priority before resuming flights. Air traffic control facilities were struggling to regain full functionality after a widespread outage that had brought US flights to a near-halt. The outdated system at the heart of the problem is being blamed for its failure, with officials pointing to ancient infrastructure as the root cause of the disruption. Old switches and routers, along with copper lines dating back to the 1980s, are said to be contributing factors in the system's collapse under pressure. Duffy had previously requested $30.1 billion from Congress to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control System, but his plea remains unheeded for now. As flights resumed, passengers continued to face delays and disruptions, with many left waiting at gates or on taxiways for hours. Desperate travelers thronged concourses, seeking information about their disrupted plans and trying to make sense of the chaos that had engulfed the country's air travel system. With thousands of flights cancelled, including some international routes, passengers were forced to consider alternative modes of transport, such as driving or rescheduling their journeys altogether. Travelers like Joseph Anderson, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California, were left scratching their heads as they tried to make sense of the situation and plan their next move. The nationwide ground stop on Friday sent shockwaves through airports across the country, leaving many travelers in a state of uncertainty. It's worth noting that such stops are extremely rare, with only two instances in recent history: January 2023 and September 2001 following the 9/11 attacks. In both cases, flights were grounded for an extended period, causing significant disruptions to air travel. According to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, there was no evidence of any hostile action on Friday, ruling out a cyberattack or AI-related incident as the cause. He also dismissed any connection with the Microsoft outage that affected millions worldwide earlier in the week. Airports across the country were severely impacted by the stop, causing frustration among travelers who had been planning their trips for days. At LaGuardia Airport in New York, Tiara Johnson was trying to get to Orlando for a concert but found her plans constantly delayed. As travelers struggled to make sense of the situation, some reported being told that wind conditions were the reason for their flight delays, while others were left scrambling to gather information about their flights. Air travel slowly returned to normal as flights resumed, but many passengers remained stuck on the ground due to a series of unexpected disruptions. Airport boards displayed departures leaving as scheduled, while mobile boarding passes indicated that flights were indeed underway, causing further confusion among stranded travelers. At Las Vegas airport, long lines formed at rental car counters as people scrambled to find alternative transportation. Passengers who had already boarded their flights were forced to disembark when staff announced a problem, leaving them to wait in lengthy queues for rental cars or other arrangements. For some, the delay proved a blessing in disguise, allowing them to extend their vacation and enjoy an extra night of relaxation with friends.
